::: {#thm-loop-invariant}
#### The loop invariant theorem

Let $I$ be a statement about the variables of a `while` loop whose guard (@def-loop-guard) is $G$.
Suppose that

1. $I$ is true at the first test of the guard, and
2. whenever $I$ and $G$ are both true at a test of the guard, $I$ is true at the next test.

Then $I$ is a loop invariant (@def-loop-invariant) of the loop.
In particular, if the loop stops, then $I$ is true and $G$ is false when it stops.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

We use induction (@def-proof-by-induction) on the number of passes through the body.
For each non-negative integer $k$, let $P(k)$ be the claim

> if the body runs at least $k$ times, then $I$ is true at the test of the guard that follows the first $k$ passes.

The test that follows the first $0$ passes is the first test.

**Base case.**
$P(0)$ is hypothesis 1.

**Inductive step.**
Let $k \ge 1$, suppose $P(k - 1)$ holds, and suppose the body runs at least $k$ times.
Then it runs at least $k - 1$ times, so by $P(k - 1)$, $I$ is true at the test that follows the first $k - 1$ passes.
The $k$th pass comes right after that test, and the body runs only when the guard is true,
so $G$ is also true at that test.
By hypothesis 2, $I$ is true at the next test, which is the test that follows the first $k$ passes.
So $P(k)$ holds.

By induction, $P(k)$ holds for every $k \ge 0$.
Every test of the guard follows the first $k$ passes for some $k \ge 0$,
so $I$ is true at every test, and $I$ is a loop invariant.
The loop stops only at a test where $G$ is false,
and $I$ is true at that test too.

:::

:::
